props.title: Rocco and His Brothers
props.initialSlug: Brothers bound by blood and strife.

sections.content: Luchino Visconti's Rocco and His Brothers (1960) stands as a towering achievement of Italian neorealism evolving into operatic melodrama. The epic tale of the Parondi family migrating from rural southern Italy to industrial Milan captures the massive social upheaval of Italy's "Economic Miracle" through intensely personal drama. Alain Delon's portrayal of the noble Rocco contrasts brilliantly with Renato Salvatori's volatile Simone, while Annie Girardot delivers a devastating performance as Nadia, the woman who becomes the catalyst for the brothers' tragic conflict. The film's influence echoes through later works like The Godfather (1972) and Once Upon a Time in America (1984) in its exploration of family, loyalty, and the corrupting effects of urban life.

sections.content: The film's stunning black-and-white cinematography by Giuseppe Rotunno creates a stark urban landscape that feels both modernist and mythic. Visconti's treatment of Milan recalls the way La Notte (1961) and L'Eclisse (1962) would soon portray the city's alienating architecture. The boxing sequences, showing Simone's rise and fall, influenced countless later films including Raging Bull (1980) and The Fighter (2010), while the raw emotional confrontations between brothers established a template for family dramas that continues to resonate.

Visconti's fusion of neorealist social observation with melodramatic intensity created a new kind of epic filmmaking. The film's three-hour runtime allows for deep character development reminiscent of The Best of Youth (2003) and La Meglio Gioventù (2003). Its exploration of southern Italian migration parallels similar themes in later works like Christ Stopped at Eboli (1979) and The Tree of Wooden Clogs (1978), examining the human cost of rapid industrialization and urbanization. sections.content: The film's influence extended far beyond Italy. Martin Scorsese has cited it as a major influence, particularly in his treatment of family dynamics and urban life in Mean Streets (1973) and Goodfellas (1990). The raw emotional power of the performances inspired a generation of method actors, while the film's unflinching examination of family bonds under pressure influenced works like The Long Good Friday (1980) and A Prophet (2009).
